name: Battle of Alarcos
info: The Almohad caliph Abu Yusuf Ya'qub al-Mansur defeated King Alfonso VIII of Castile at Alarcos, near the Guadiana, on 18 July 1195, and Castile's field army was destroyed, leaving the road to Toledo open.

facts.place: Alarcos (al-Arak in Arabic), near the Guadiana River, the southern limit of the Kingdom of Castile, in what is now central Spain; the Almohad army formed around a small hill called La Cabeza, two bow-shots from Alarcos
facts.sides: The Almohads under the caliph Abu Yusuf Ya'qub al-Mansur, with his vizier Abu Yahya ibn Abi Hafs commanding the vanguard; Castile under King Alfonso VIII, whose heavy cavalry, about 8,000 strong, was led by Diego López de Haro
facts.outcome: The Almohads won; the Castilian field army was destroyed and Alfonso fled to Toledo. The garrison of the unfinished fortress of Alarcos surrendered on terms and many nearby castles fell or were abandoned.

t: Alfonso VIII marched to Alarcos without waiting for the reinforcements coming from Alfonso IX of León and Sancho VII of Navarre.
The Castilian heavy cavalry broke the Almohad front lines and killed the vizier, but the Arab left enveloped its flank and rear and al-Mansur's rearguard then attacked.
The victory proved short-lived: al-Mansur went back to Africa in 1198, and his successor Muhammad al-Nasir was defeated at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.
dyk: Pedro Fernández de Castro, who held a personal feud against Alfonso, rode with the Almohads and was sent by the caliph to negotiate the surrender of the castle of Alarcos.
ev: Al-Mansur recaptures Silves from Portugal and returns to his capital, and an armistice with the Christian kings follows
At the end of the truce Alfonso invades southern al-Andalus, led by the Archbishop of Toledo and the Order of Calatrava
Al-Mansur lands at Tarifa on 1 June and reaches Córdoba on 30 June
The Almohad army crosses the Muradal pass and destroys a Christian cavalry detachment, while Alfonso marches from Toledo to Alarcos

sections.background:
In 1190 the Almohad caliph al-Mansur travelled from North Africa to al-Andalus to invade Portugal, which had captured the city of Silves the year before. After a campaign of about 15 months he recaptured the city in July 1191 and returned to his capital. An armistice between the Almohads and the Christian kings of Castile and León followed.

When the truce expired in 1194, Alfonso VIII of Castile decided to invade Almohad territory in southern al-Andalus, including the heartland of the Guadalquivir River. He struck then because he had learned that al-Mansur was gravely ill and that the caliph's brother Abu Yahya, the governor of al-Andalus, had gone to Marrakesh to claim the Almohad throne for himself. The invasion was led for Alfonso by Martín López de Pisuerga, the Archbishop of Toledo, supported by the military Order of Calatrava. In Marrakesh al-Mansur recovered, reasserted his control over his brother and began to plan an expedition into al-Andalus against the Christian invaders.
sections.forces:
On 1 June 1195 al-Mansur landed at Tarifa. His main army passed through the province of Seville and reached Córdoba on 30 June, reinforced by the troops of local governors and by a Christian cavalry contingent under Pedro Fernández de Castro, who held a personal feud against Alfonso. On 4 July al-Mansur left Córdoba and went through the Muradal pass into the Campo de Calatrava, the fertile plain dominated by the fortress of Salvatierra. On the way his forces intercepted and surrounded a Christian cavalry detachment that was tracking the Muslim army, and only a handful of scouts escaped to report to Alfonso.

Alfonso gathered his forces at Toledo and marched to Alarcos, near the Guadiana, which marked the southern limit of his kingdom and where a fortress was under construction. He meant to bar access to the rich Tagus valley, and he did not wait for the reinforcements on their way from Alfonso IX of León and Sancho VII of Navarre. He put most of his heavy cavalry, about 8,000 strong, in a compact group under Diego López de Haro, lord of Vizcaya, and he himself was to follow with the infantry and the Military Orders. Alfonso had badly underestimated the Almohad host.

Al-Mansur gave his vizier, Abu Yahya ibn Abi Hafs, command of a strong vanguard. In its first line were the Bani Marin volunteers under Abu Jalil Mahyu ibn Abi Bakr, with many archers, and the Zenata tribe. Behind them stood the vizier with the Amir's banner and his personal guard, from the Hintata tribe. The Arab hosts under Yarmun ibn Riyah were on the left and the forces of al-Andalus under the Caid Ibn Sanadid on the right. Al-Mansur held the rearguard himself, the best Almohad forces, with the black African guard.
sections.course:
The Almohad host came into view on 16 July, but al-Mansur did not accept battle at once, preferring to rest his forces. On Wednesday 18 July the Almohad army formed for battle around a small hill called La Cabeza, two bow-shots from Alarcos. Alfonso chose to move first and ordered his forces down from their high position, with the heavy cavalry charging across the lower plain.

At the outset the battle went well for the Christians. After striking the Muslim front lines, the knights began a three-hour engagement in which they first dispersed the Bani Marin and the Zenata, then attacked the Hintata and killed the vizier Abu Yahya, and finally fought against the forces of al-Andalus under Ibn Sanadid and routed them. As the Christians fought, tired and fell, the Arab left under Yarmun enveloped their flank and rear. The Almohad rearguard under al-Mansur then attacked and surrounded the Christian knights.

Alfonso advanced with all his remaining forces into the melee and found himself assaulted from all sides under a rain of arrows. He fought hand to hand for some time until his bodyguard removed him from the action, almost by force, and together they fled to Toledo. The Castilian infantry was destroyed, together with most of the Orders that had supported it. The lord of Vizcaya tried to force his way through the ring of enemies but had to take refuge in the unfinished fortress of Alarcos with only a fraction of his knights.
sections.aftermath:
The castle was surrounded, with some 3,000 people trapped inside, half of them women and children. The Amir sent Pedro Fernández de Castro, who had taken little part in the fighting, to negotiate the surrender. López de Haro and the survivors were allowed to go, leaving 12 knights as hostages for the payment of a great ransom.

The Castilian field army had been destroyed. The dead included three bishops, from Ávila, Segovia and Sigüenza; Count Ordoño García de Roda and his brothers; Counts Pedro Ruiz de Guzmán and Rodrigo Sánchez; and the Masters of the Order of Santiago, Sancho Fernández de Lemus, and of the Portuguese Order of St Benedict, Gonçalo Viegas. Muslim losses included the vizier, and Abu Jalil Mahyu ibn Abi Bakr, commander of the Bani Marin volunteers, who died of his wounds in the following year. Al-Mansur also suffered considerable losses.

The outcome shook the stability of Castile for several years. All the nearby castles surrendered or were abandoned, among them Malagón, Benavente, Calatrava, Caracuel and Torre de Guadalferza, which left the passage to Toledo wide open. Al-Mansur went back to Seville to make good his losses and took the title al-Mansur Billah, 'The one victorious by God'. For two years his forces devastated Extremadura, the Tagus valley, La Mancha and the country around Toledo, and moved against Montánchez, Trujillo, Plasencia, Talavera, Escalona and Maqueda; some of these expeditions were led by Pedro Fernández de Castro. Almohad diplomacy won an alliance with Alfonso IX of León, who had been enraged that Alfonso VIII did not wait for him, and the neutrality of Navarre. Both arrangements proved temporary. In 1198 the caliph, in poor health, returned to Africa, and he died in February 1199.
sections.sources:
The Almohad order of battle is known commander by commander and tribe by tribe, and the Christian dead are known by name and title. Of the armies' strengths only two figures stand: the 8,000 heavy cavalry under López de Haro and the 3,000 people in the castle.

What followed is told in two ways. The raids after the battle are said to have brought the caliph no territorial gains, and it is also said that the Almohads reconquered Trujillo, Montánchez and Talavera. The commander of the Bani Marin volunteers is said to have died of his wounds a year later.
sections.legacy:
The success of the battle proved short-lived. The raids that followed brought the caliph no territorial gains, the alliances his diplomacy won with León and Navarre lasted only a time, and he lost interest in the affairs of the Iberian Peninsula. His aim of keeping a hold over al-Andalus appeared to be a complete success when he left in 1198.

Sixteen years after Alarcos the Almohad caliph Muhammad al-Nasir tried to build on it with a new Iberian offensive and was defeated at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212. That battle was a turning point that led to the end of Moorish rule in the Iberian Peninsula. The Almohad Caliphate itself collapsed a few decades later.

For Castile the immediate legacy was the loss of its southern frontier. Alarcos had marked the southern limit of the kingdom, and the surrender or abandonment of Malagón, Benavente, Calatrava, Caracuel and Torre de Guadalferza left the passage to Toledo wide open, while the raids of the following two years reached the country around Toledo itself. The defeat also strained relations among the Christian kingdoms: Alfonso IX of León, enraged that Alfonso VIII had not waited for him, allied with the Almohads for a time, and Navarre stayed neutral. Al-Mansur, by contrast, took the title al-Mansur Billah after the victory.

summary: At Alarcos on 18 July 1195 the Almohad caliph al-Mansur defeated Alfonso VIII of Castile, destroyed his field army and left the road to Toledo open. The gains were brief, and the Almohads were beaten at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.
notes: The article contradicts itself on territory: the lead says the Almohads reconquered Trujillo, Montánchez and Talavera, the Aftermath says the raids led to no territorial gains. The sections give the Aftermath's version and name the three places only as targets of raids.
The lead says 'Trujillo ... reconquered'; the body says the forces 'moved against' them. Left as 'moved against'.
The article gives no total strengths and no casualty figures; only the 8,000 cavalry and the 3,000 trapped in the castle.
The article names no chronicle or author, so the sources section is thin by necessity.
'Abi Bakr' in the casualty paragraph is read as Abu Jalil Mahyu ibn Abi Bakr, the Bani Marin commander named earlier; the article does not link them in so many words.
The article's phrase 'almost annihilated' for the scouting detachment was left as 'intercepted and surrounded'.
Date given as 18 July in the lead and as Wednesday in the body; no dispute stated.
